skill.description: Guide authorized ffuf-based DAST testing for web applications, including content discovery, parameter fuzzing, virtual host checks, filtering, and reporting practices.
skill.summary: Guide authorized ffuf web fuzzing for application security testing.
skill.author: AgentSecOps

security_audit.summary: Most static alerts are Markdown examples, placeholder URLs, or reference text, but the review confirms a critical CI supply-chain issue and high-risk dual-use DAST guidance. The skill is useful for authorized application security testing, yet it can enable reconnaissance, credential enumeration, and sensitive file discovery if used outside scope.

remediation.issue: Remote installer is piped directly to bash in the CI template.
remediation.suggestion: Replace curl-to-shell installation with a pinned release, checksum verification, or a trusted package source.

remediation.issue: CI examples use mutable third-party action references and pass GITHUB_TOKEN to a third-party action.
remediation.suggestion: Pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs, restrict token permissions, and document required token scopes.

remediation.issue: Authentication fuzzing guidance can enable account enumeration or brute-force behavior.
remediation.suggestion: Add explicit authorization, test-account, rate-limit, lockout, and stop-condition requirements before any credential testing.

remediation.issue: Sensitive file discovery guidance includes downloading and analyzing discovered files.
remediation.suggestion: Require scope confirmation, minimize data access, avoid downloading sensitive content unless approved, and document handling rules.
Reword the section to emphasize service stability, consent, and safety rather than avoiding detection.

content.value_statement: Hidden web paths and weak endpoint behavior are hard to test consistently. This skill guides authorized ffuf workflows for discovery, parameter fuzzing, and evidence-based reporting.
actual_capabilities: Explains ffuf setup and common installation paths.
Guides directory, file, API, and virtual host discovery.
Shows GET, POST, header, cookie, and extension fuzzing patterns.
Covers ffuf filtering, matching, recursion, modes, and output formats.
Maps testing activity to OWASP Web Security Testing Guide areas.
Provides CI and reporting examples for security scan results.
limitations: Does not verify that a target is authorized for testing.
Requires ffuf, wordlists, and network access configured outside the skill.
Can generate high request volume if users ignore rate limits.
Does not replace manual validation or legal review.

use_cases.title: Test Web Content Exposure
use_cases.description: Plan scoped directory, file, and API discovery for an authorized web application.

use_cases.title: Add DAST to CI
use_cases.description: Build repeatable staging checks with ffuf output handling and security reporting steps.

use_cases.title: Validate Bug Bounty Scope
use_cases.description: Tune fuzzing against program-approved hosts while keeping evidence clear and reproducible.

prompt_templates.title: Start Directory Discovery
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner authorized test against one web host.
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan a safe ffuf directory discovery pass for this authorized target: [target]. Include wordlist choice, filters, and evidence to collect.

prompt_templates.title: Tune Fuzzing Filters
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate review of noisy ffuf results.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these ffuf result patterns: [summary]. Recommend status, size, word, and line filters that reduce false positives without hiding useful findings.

prompt_templates.title: Plan Authentication Testing
prompt_templates.prompt: Design an authorized authentication endpoint fuzzing plan for [application]. Include scope limits, rate limits, lockout safety, and manual validation steps.

prompt_templates.title: Design CI DAST Workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a CI DAST workflow using ffuf for staging only. Include trigger rules, artifacts, failure criteria, and safeguards against excessive traffic.

output_examples.input: Authorized staging site needs content discovery before release.
output: Start with a small common content wordlist and only approved staging hosts.
Filter obvious baseline responses before expanding coverage.
Record discovered paths, response status, size, and manual validation notes.

output_examples.input: Noisy ffuf run returns many similar responses.
output: Compare a known missing path against interesting responses.
Use response size and word count filters to remove the baseline pattern.
Keep redirects, forbidden responses, and unusual sizes for manual review.

output_examples.input: Team wants authentication endpoint testing in scope.
output: Confirm written permission, account lockout rules, and test account ownership first.
Use low concurrency and strict request limits.
Report enumeration signals only after manual verification.

best_practices: Confirm written authorization and exact target scope before any fuzzing.
Start with small wordlists and low concurrency, then expand carefully.
Validate every finding manually before assigning severity or impact.
anti_patterns: Fuzzing public or third-party systems without permission.
Treating every 200 or 403 response as a confirmed vulnerability.
Running large credential wordlists against production login forms.

faq.question: What is this skill for?
faq.answer: It helps plan and interpret authorized ffuf-based DAST testing for web applications.

faq.question: Does it include ffuf itself?
faq.answer: No. Users must install ffuf and provide wordlists in their own environment.

faq.question: Can it test third-party sites?
faq.answer: Only when the user has written permission and the target is inside the approved scope.

faq.question: What results can it help analyze?
faq.answer: It can help interpret status codes, response sizes, filters, discovered paths, and validation priorities.

faq.question: Can it run credential attacks?
faq.answer: It discusses authentication fuzzing only for controlled, authorized tests with strict limits.

faq.question: How should teams reduce operational risk?
faq.answer: Use staging targets, low concurrency, small wordlists, rate limits, and clear stop conditions.
